## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Sacred Number 10: Completion, Ending, Turning Point, The End of the Old and the Beginning of the New**

**2. Belongs to the Fire Element**

Many people think "fate" is predestined and that you can only passively accept it. But the involvement of the **fire element** directly rewrites this logic. What does fire represent? It represents **action, transformation, and divine will**.

**Jupiter is the "Great Benefic" and also the "Propeller":** Jupiter brings not only good luck but also a kind of **expansive driving force**. Just like a rocket needs boosters to launch, the turning of the Wheel of Fortune is actually the universe **"adding fuel"** for you.

**Not "going with the flow," but "actively intervening":** Water element flows along, fire element **pushes forward**. When the Wheel of Fortune appears, it often doesn't mean you lie down and wait for good things to happen; it tells you: **"The current wind direction is favorable to you, set sail quickly!"**

**The Sphinx with the body of a lion at the top:** It is a **lion**, the king of fire signs. It sits at the **top** of the wheel, holding a sword. This indicates that the turning of the Wheel of Fortune is not random. It has **direction** and **wisdom**. The sphinx uses the fire of wisdom to control the direction of the wheel.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=M2RjMjQ4ZTUyMDQ2NzFlODFkZjdhNjI2NGViOGQxNThfNzZhYzQxODUyOTdjYWU5MzYwMjg2NjNjMmQyMzQwNjFfSUQ6NzYxOTIzMzg3MTU4NjQ5NTY3OF8xNzgyMTgxNDA0OjE3ODIyNjc4MDRfVjM)

**3. Astrological Correspondence: Jupiter**

In the **Golden Dawn system**, the 22 Major Arcana correspond to 22 Hebrew letters, as well as planets and zodiac signs.

The Wheel of Fortune (Card 10) is precisely assigned to **Jupiter**. This is not an isolated symbolic game but a complete **cosmic model**. From ancient times to the present, true sages have known: **the turning of the Wheel of Fortune must involve "divine power."** And Jupiter is the god who provides that "driving force."

Jupiter is the largest planet, representing **expansion, law, and philosophy**. Many people think Jupiter means "easy wins," but that is somewhat misleading.

1. **Jupiter is cyclical**

Jupiter takes about 12 years to orbit the sun, and it governs the **rhythm of time**.

Why does the Wheel of Fortune turn? Because **the time has come**.

Like bamboo, it may only grow a few centimeters in the first four years, but its underground roots spread wildly. In the fifth year, it grows at a speed of 30 centimeters per day.

**Jupiter is the season that makes you "grow wildly" and "explode."**

The previous dormancy was not wasted; now is the time to burst forth.

2. **Jupiter is the judge of "cause and effect"**

Jupiter is the god of law and morality.

The inscription on the Wheel of Fortune reads: "I rule, I am ruling, I lose power, I will rule again."

This shows the **wheel turns with reason**.

The causes you planted before—effort, altruism, accumulation—when they reach Jupiter, it must give you results.

**Jupiter's "good luck" is essentially the fruition of the "virtue" you have accumulated.**

The so-called "help from benefactors" is just Jupiter helping you settle the interest.

3. **Jupiter has a global perspective**

Jupiter rules Sagittarius (exploration) and Pisces (faith).

When the Wheel of Fortune reaches its peak, you don't see just immediate gains or losses but the **whole script**.

Like when we create intellectual property, sometimes short-term looks like a loss (content no one watches), but long-term, you are building trust assets.

**Jupiter's energy lets you step out of the game and see life from a god's-eye view.** This is part of the script.

**At Jupiter's "low point" (wheel turning downward):** Accumulate like a hermit, learn, and settle. This is Jupiter giving you time to "crouch and spring."

**At Jupiter's "peak" (wheel turning upward):** You must expand like an emperor. When opportunities come, charge forward; when benefactors appear, cling to them; when there is traffic, monetize fiercely.

**Always maintain a "philosophical height":** Accept impermanence. Do not be arrogant in prosperity, nor discouraged in adversity. Because **this is only one phase of Jupiter's cycle.**

**4. Hebrew Letter: The Grasping Hand**

The Wheel of Fortune corresponds to the Hebrew letter Yod (י),

Yod is the 10th letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

Its shape is extremely simple: a small dot or a slightly curved hook, like a finger, a spark, or an outstretched hand.

Its numerical value is 10, corresponding to Tarot card number 10—the Wheel of Fortune.

Yod is traditionally interpreted as the "Divine Hand" or "Grasping Hand"—symbolizing the active intervention of divine will in fate.

It means grasping fate, actively confronting destiny.

## 3. Case Studies

The Forbidden City’s feng shui nurtures people, yet in *Empresses in the Palace* no one becomes a true winner.

Everyone thinks they are the helmsman, but in reality, they are just a speck of dust under the wheel of fate.

When Zhen Huan first entered the palace, her eyes were clear, believing in "wishing to find a devoted partner to grow old together." But the emperor’s words "Gentle and like you" nailed her to the position of a substitute. She wanted to withdraw, but those five words shattered her completely. Later, returning as Consort Xi, she advanced step by step, seemingly successful in revenge, but she personally married her own daughter Hongyue off to the Zunghar—while the phrase "If the princess loses the emperor’s favor, what will she do in the future?" was exactly what she once used to intimidate Cao Qinmo.

Now the fate line is pulled tight, forming a closed loop.

Consort Hua was arrogant all her life, believing her favor would never fade, but she did not know that the fragrant incense she burned daily was a sterilization poison jointly set by the emperor and empress dowager. She only realized at death: her love was nothing but a carefully woven imperial cage—even her tears were props in the script.

An Lingrong climbed desperately not for power but to be seen and respected. Yet whether she sided with the empress, used spices to harm others, or competed for favor with ice games, she was always a disposable pawn in others’ hands. In the cold palace, swallowing bitter apricot seeds, she murmured before death: "My whole life was just a joke."

Her tragedy was never about lacking ruthlessness but that her birth and fate had already written her ending—in this palace, some people’s very existence seems superfluous.

Only Consort Duan, after being given safflower by Consort Hua and rendered infertile for life, chose silent dormancy. She neither cried nor made a fuss, but used strength against strength and ultimately survived to the end. She saw through it: "You cannot control the wind direction, but you can adjust the sails."

This is not compromise but clarity. Allowing everything to happen is the only way not to be crushed by impermanence.

More absurdly, even goodwill can turn into tragedy.

The poison antidote chopsticks sent by the Peiguo Duke Meng’s family, while his daughter Meng Jingxian died from testing poison for Zhen Huan, ironically became Zhen Huan’s poison-avoiding chopsticks.

Goodwill made a full circle and became fate’s coldest mockery.

And that bowl of "pregnancy medicine." Consort Duan personally handed it to Consort Hua with a concerned face. But the medicine concealed the emperor and empress dowager’s assassination plot. Consort Hua miscarried, hated Consort Duan to death, never knowing the truth.

Trust at this moment was sharper than a dagger.

The love between Prince Guo and Zhen Huan was as brilliant as wildflowers.

His words "I don’t want to be a prince" were a wholehearted renunciation;

Her words "No matter how cold, you shouldn’t warm yourself with someone else’s blood" were a bone-deep restraint.

But even the deepest love could not overcome the triple iron walls of identity, timing, and imperial power.

They loved purely and lost completely—simply because they were born in the wrong era and stood in the wrong place.

Throughout the drama, the sense of fate is like a thin mist, growing thicker as it goes on.

Looking back at those understated lines, each word is like a prophecy:

"Pink and tender, how old are you now?"

—Youthful innocence will fade; growing up is disillusionment.

"Wearing lake blue and sapphire green must match your status."

—Status determines fate; colors are also shackles.

"I don’t want to be Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai; one cried at her wedding, the other died early from blood vomiting."

—Love before power is just a footnote to tragedy.

Zhen Huan ultimately sat on the empress dowager’s throne, crowned phoenix, above all. But Mei Zhuang died, Prince Guo died, Liu Zhu died young protecting her, Hongyue was married off to the frontier.

She won the harem but lost all worldly warmth. The price of victory was the desolation of the soul.

A recent phrase sums it up well:

The highest form of inner strength in *Empresses in the Palace* is "allowing everything to happen."

This is not passive resignation but choosing to live clearly after seeing the impermanence of the world.

The Wheel of Fortune rolls forward; no one can defy fate.

But some can stand firm in the storm—

Like Consort Duan, like Zhen Huan (later).

They no longer ask "Why me?" but "What should I do next?"

This may be the deepest lesson *Empresses in the Palace* leaves for modern people:

**The world is inherently impermanent; the human heart can hold steady.**
